_rule: Every dated result and milestone, once. CANON/results_to_tex.py writes the book's development chapter (docs/book/part6/p6_25_development.tex) and the Advancements table of Biological_Physics/README.md from this file; numbers are recomputed from the committed records, never typed. status: development | commissioned | withdrawn. A result moves out of the development chapter only by changing its status here; CANON/status_check.py refuses a push while the book or README differs from what this file generates, or while a record and this file disagree about commissioning. Every kind=commissioning entry lists in 'covers' the development results its commissioning closes; the gate refuses while any covered result is still status development.

entries.title: Cancer fingerprint: prostate, both instruments on the same cells
entries.plain: Our two instruments look at DNA's switch pattern in two different ways. One counts scattered single errors, like typos in a book. The other checks whether the pattern as a whole is still intact. If cancer only made a cell sloppier, both readings would rise together, in a proportion physics sets in advance. A fingerprint is when the pattern is damaged far more than the typos explain: whole passages are gone, not just letters. Here we compared prostate cancer cells with normal prostate cells, with the rule for calling a fingerprint written down before any cancer data were opened, and every cancer sample carried it.

win.head: The cancer fingerprint, in prostate cancer
win.sub: Whole stretches of the DNA's switch pattern wiped out, far beyond the everyday wear healthy cells show, seen by both of our instruments on the same cells.

entries.title: IAM-A, first physics lever: cutting the methyl supply
entries.plain: A test of the physics itself, in living animals. The cell needs a chemical supply to keep its DNA switches set. In mice that cannot make that supply in the liver, the physics predicts how much faithfulness the liver's DNA pattern should lose. That window was calculated and sealed on a healthy mouse before any of these mice were read, and the mice landed inside it. Giving the supply back moved them back toward healthy.

win.head: Physics called it in advance, in living mice
win.sub: We wrote down where the reading must land if the methyl supply is cut ({low:.3f} to {high:.3f}). The mice read {ratio:.3f}, inside the window.

entries.title: Met-A reproduces across laboratories on identical DNA
entries.plain: Can anyone trust the number? Exactly the same DNA was measured in three different laboratories. Our reading came out the same in all three, within a small fraction of a percent, before any correction. A measurement that changes from lab to lab is useless; this one does not.

win.head: The same DNA gives the same answer in three laboratories
win.sub: Identical reference DNA, {arrays} arrays across {labs} laboratories, read alike by Met-A.

entries.title: Met-A raises no false alarm when foreign DNA is mixed in
entries.plain: A false-alarm test. Small amounts of DNA from other organs (liver, lung, colon, brain) were mixed into blood DNA in known amounts. Healthy foreign DNA should not look like disease, and it did not: every mixed sample read healthy.

win.head: No false alarms
win.sub: Foreign DNA mixed into healthy blood: every mixture still read healthy.

entries.headline: **Met-A on isolated neutrophils (EPIC v1) commissioned**, with its detection limit printed on every report
entries.plain: Commissioned means a reading is allowed to report results, not just development readings. For Met-A on purified white blood cells (neutrophils), the tests for repeatability, agreement between laboratories, no false alarms on healthy samples, refusing what it cannot read, and responding to known damage by the predicted amount were all met. Its sensitivity to the very smallest damage fell short of the bar, so instead of hiding that, every report prints its measured detection limit: the smallest damage it reliably sees.

win.sub: Met-A on white blood cells passed every test written for it before its data was read.

entries.title: Met-A on patients' breast tumors against their own normal tissue
entries.plain: Real patients, not lab cells. Each woman's breast tumor was compared with her own healthy breast tissue, processed on the same plate, reading only places on the DNA that a change in the mix of tissue types cannot move, so a different mix cannot fake a result. The bar was strict: healthy tissue crosses it only about one time in twenty. Far more tumors crossed it than chance could produce, and most tumors read above the patient's own healthy tissue. This shows the measurement sees breast cancer in patients as a group; flagging each individual patient reliably is the next step.

win.head: Breast cancer: patients' tumors leave the healthy range far more often than chance
win.sub: Each woman's tumor was read against her own healthy breast tissue. Chance alone puts about {exp} of {n} outside the healthy range; {k} were, and {up} of {n} tumors read above the woman's own tissue. The rule was sealed before a single tumor was opened.

entries.title: Met-A on patients' colorectal tumors against their own adjacent normal
entries.plain: The same design as the breast test, in colorectal cancer: each patient's tumor against the same patient's healthy colon from next to it, on the same processing slide, at places the tissue mix cannot move, with a strict bar fixed in advance. Far more tumors crossed it than chance would give, and nearly every tumor read above the patient's own healthy tissue.

win.head: Colorectal cancer: the same signal, in a second cancer
win.sub: Chance alone puts about {exp} of {n} outside the healthy range; {k} were, and {up} of {n} tumors read above the patient's own healthy colon. Sealed in advance, scored once.

entries.title: Cancer fingerprint replicated: prostate, a second laboratory, different cells
entries.plain: The same prostate test, repeated on data from a different laboratory, with different normal prostate cells as the comparison. Every cancer sample again carried the fingerprint (whole passages of the switch pattern wiped out), and even the weakest one stood well clear of the difference between two healthy people. A result that repeats in a second laboratory, on different cells, is much harder to explain away.

win.head: Found again: the fingerprint in a second laboratory's prostate cancer
win.sub: Different cells, a different lab, every cancer sample. The weakest still {ratio:.1f} times the difference between two healthy people.

entries.title: Cancer fingerprint in breast cancer cell lines
entries.plain: Two breast cancer cell lines, each compared with two kinds of normal breast cells, one comparison at a time, each sealed before it was read. Cancer can damage the pattern in two directions: switches lost where they should be on, and switches added where they should be off. The meter for added switches found the breast cancer fingerprint in every comparison; the meter for lost switches found it in most, and one was undecided.

win.head: Breast cancer cell lines carry a fingerprint of their own
win.sub: Seen in every comparison with normal breast cells.

entries.title: Met-A on patients' liver tumors against their own normal liver
entries.plain: Real patients with liver cancer. Each patient's liver tumor was compared with that same patient's healthy liver, processed on the same plate, reading only places on the DNA that a change in the mix of tissue types cannot move. Before any tumor was opened, we also checked that no realistic change in the mix of cells could fake a result. The bar was strict: healthy liver crosses it only about one time in twenty. Far more tumors crossed it than chance could produce, and nearly every tumor read above the patient's own healthy liver. This shows the measurement sees liver cancer in patients as a group; flagging each individual patient reliably, and seeing it in blood, are the next steps.

win.head: Liver cancer: a third cancer, the same result
win.sub: Chance alone puts about {exp} of {n} outside the healthy range; {k} were, and {up} of {n} tumors read above the patient's own healthy liver.

entries.title: The clustering meter's healthy range holds in two new laboratories
entries.plain: Our second meter, the clustering meter, reads the shape of the damage: whether errors clump together, as they do when a whole region is wiped, or stay scattered, as ordinary errors do. Its healthy range was set on other laboratories' arrays and committed before two new laboratories' healthy blood was read. In both, at least 95 percent of healthy people had to read inside the range, and they did. The second laboratory passed by a single array, and both are whole blood rather than the purified cells the meter is being commissioned on, so this is development, not commissioning.

win.head: Our second meter's healthy range holds in new laboratories
win.sub: {in1} of {n1} and {in2} of {n2} healthy people inside a range set before either laboratory was read (bar: 95 percent). The second passed by one array.

Every number our commissioned instrument uses came out identical. The rebuild also found two hidden inputs (an unpinned software version and the chip maker's files), which are now pinned and checked on every run.

entries.title: Every healthy cell follows the same simple rule
entries.plain: Your cells put tiny chemical tags on their DNA. The tags tell each cell what kind of cell it is. Some stretches of DNA are tagged firmly and some loosely, and every cell makes a few tagging mistakes. We looked at 56 kinds of healthy human cells and found that the number of mistakes depends on one thing: how much of its DNA the cell keeps loosely tagged. Plotted, all 56 fall on one straight line. So we can tell what a healthy cell should look like from that cell's own sample, without comparing it to a library of other cells. Early result, from one laboratory's data. Next, we check it in a second lab.

win.head: Every healthy cell follows the same simple rule
win.sub: Cells tag their DNA to remember what kind of cell they are, and make a few tagging mistakes. Across {n} kinds of healthy human cells, the number of mistakes depends on one thing: how much of the DNA the cell keeps loosely tagged. So what a healthy cell should look like comes from its own sample, not a library of other cells. Early result, one laboratory's data; a second lab is next.

entries.headline: **Every healthy cell follows the same simple rule.** Across 56 kinds of healthy human cells, the number of DNA-tagging mistakes depends on one thing, how much of the DNA the cell keeps loosely tagged, so a healthy cell's expected reading comes from its own sample (early result, one laboratory)

entries.title: The clustering meter passes its last check: the same person reads the same
entries.plain: Our second meter reads the shape of the damage: clumps, as a tumor leaves, or scattered, as ordinary wear leaves. Its last open check was whether one person measured twice reads the same. We found a public study, never touched by this work, in which 14 healthy adults were measured twice on different chips. The bar, set before the arrays were read, allowed a spread of 0.125; the meter's spread was 0.038, about a third of that. The same 173 arrays were also a third laboratory for its healthy range, and 172 read inside it. Every check in its plan is now met, and it is proposed for commissioning on whole blood. Its detection of clumped damage has been shown on changes planted into real arrays, not yet on real tumors.

win.head: The clustering meter passes its last check
win.sub: The same person measured twice reads the same (spread {sd:.3f}, bar {bar}); a third laboratory's healthy blood read inside its range ({inn} of {n}). Proposed for commissioning.

entries.headline: **The clustering meter (C-score) commissioned** on whole blood (EPIC v1), with its band and detection limit printed on every report
entries.plain: Commissioned means a reading is allowed to report results, not just development readings. The clustering meter reads the shape of the damage: clumps, as a tumor leaves, or scattered, as ordinary wear leaves. Every test written for it before its data were read was met: its healthy range held in three laboratories that never helped set it, the same person measured twice reads the same, and clumped damage planted into real healthy arrays was caught every time while scattered damage never set it off. It is our second commissioned instrument, on whole blood; purified white cells are its next scope step. It has not yet read real tumors with a sealed bar; that is its next test.

win.head: Our second instrument is commissioned: the clustering meter
win.sub: It reads not how much a blood sample's DNA tags have changed, but how: scattered like ordinary wear, or packed together the way a tumor leaves them. It passed every test written for it before its data was read, in three independent laboratories.

story.p: Most methylation tests ask how much a sample has changed. The clustering meter asks how it changed. Ordinary aging leaves small changes spread thinly across the genome. A tumor that silences or loses a whole region leaves its changes packed together in stretches. Two samples can carry the same amount of change and mean very different things, and this meter tells them apart from a single blood array.

It is one of the tools we carried over from cosmology. Cosmologists subtract the sky they expect to see and measure how the leftover departures cluster; that measurement is how the Planck mission pinned down what the universe is made of and how old it is. We subtract a healthy cell's expected pattern from a sample and measure the same thing along the genome, in order: whether the leftovers clump. The same leftovers can be drawn on a sphere, the way a microwave sky is drawn.

Not as far as we can find. Other groups count how many sites in a person's blood are unusual compared with other people. That is a count. The clustering meter is a different instrument: it asks whether one sample's departures from healthy sit together along the genome, reads that on a fixed healthy band checked in independent laboratories, and prints a call and a detection limit for every sample.

The healthy range was set on 617 healthy arrays from 19 studies, then fixed. Three laboratories that had no part in setting it read 34 of 35, 22 of 23 and 172 of 173 healthy bloods inside it. Thirteen people measured twice on different chips read the same to within 0.038, against an allowance of 0.125. Clumped damage planted into real healthy arrays was caught every time; scattered damage never set it off.
Reading real tumors with a bar fixed in advance, so we learn where on its scale a tumor begins; then purified white cells from an independent laboratory, older and newer array types, and plasma.

entries.title: The C-Score commissioned on whole blood
IAM-Atlas v2.1 against the published array reference atlas of human cell types, on the jobs a reference atlas is used for
entries.plain: A reference atlas is used for two jobs: finding the DNA spots that mark each cell type, and working out which cells a mixed sample came from. On healthy cells from laboratories that never helped build either atlas, v2.1 was scored against the published array reference atlas of human cell types by bars sealed before v2.1 existed. It found as many reliable markers, split blood-cell mixtures with a smaller error, and, when brain cells that reference does not hold were mixed in, recovered them and cut the error by more than half.

win.head: Our atlas beats the field's reference on its own jobs
win.sub: On {n} held-out arrays: blood mixtures split {less} percent more accurately than the published array reference; brain cells it does not hold recovered in {rec} percent of mixtures.

entries.headline: **IAM-Atlas v2.1 commissioned** for three cell references and the colon and lung tissue tests' blind sites, each on a bar sealed before the atlas existed
entries.plain: Commissioned means a use of the atlas is allowed to report results. Healthy cells from laboratories that never helped build the atlas were read against it, by bars fixed before it existed. Three cell types, brain neurons, airway lining and naive helper T cells, landed inside the atlas's predicted range, and the sites the colon and lung cancer tests depend on held steady in every cell type that could be checked. Its blood-composition use and its other cell references stay in development.

win.sub: Three cell references and the sites behind our colon and lung cancer tests passed bars fixed before the atlas existed; on the jobs a reference atlas is used for, it also beat the field's published reference.

entries.title: IAM-Atlas v2.1 commissioned
IAM-Atlas v2.1 against the published sequencing atlas of human cell types, on the jobs a reference atlas is used for
entries.plain: The published sequencing atlas was rebuilt for arrays exactly as its paper builds it, from its 205 public samples, and scored against v2.1 by the same sealed bars v2.1 met against the published array reference. On 731 healthy arrays from laboratories that never helped build either atlas, v2.1's markers held more often (0.998 against 0.938), it split mixtures with a smaller error (0.020 against 0.025), and with brain cells that atlas does not hold mixed in, it cut the error by half (0.023 against 0.048).

entries.title: IAM-A commissioned: each sample read against its own reference

losses.plain: Our second instrument's commissioning is on hold. Reading identical reference DNA, four of its five checks passed; the fifth, agreement between two laboratories on one kit, did not. By our own stopping rule that holds the whole commissioning until we find out why. The test that is running tonight is that search.

Lung cancer, four times. One set of patients read no clear cancer signal. Three more were stopped by our own made-up tests before a single tumor was opened, because ordinary differences between people's lungs could have faked a result. No tumor data was spent.
A colorectal replication set was ruled unsuitable. Its patients' normal tissue varied too much for the test to decide anything, and we said so instead of running it.

A drug experiment gave no result. Decitabine lowers methylation by a known amount, so it should have been a clean check of the link between our two instruments. At the dose that could decide it, too few molecules were readable.
Two tests of how the copying enzyme chooses its targets: one not confirmed, one not met. Both were written down in advance and both are in the record.

A second physics lever was parked before we downloaded anything. Starving cells of methionine should raise the reading, but in the only public experiment the cells had nearly stopped dividing, so the calculation showed it could not decide the question.

Our first proposed fix for the instrument's laboratory failure did not work, and we found out on made-up data before spending any real files. The idea was to read three places in each sequencing file instead of one and add them together. Tested against runs with a known answer and a bent beginning, it cut the error from about 15 percent to about 5 percent - but our tolerance is 3 percent, because averaging in a bad measurement makes it smaller, not absent. The fix has to exclude the untrustworthy part of the file, decided from the machine's own quality numbers rather than from our result. Recorded as tried and failed.

A new instrument idea passed its physics test and failed its practical one, on made-up data, before any real sample was used. The idea: compare how damaged the hard-to-maintain parts of the genome are against the easy parts, within one sample, so that everything affecting the whole sample cancels out. The physics prediction held to one percent - we calculated the expected ratio in advance from healthy samples with nothing fitted. But the cancellation only works for one kind of nuisance; a change in which cells are present scales everything proportionally and survives, at about five times the size of the signal we were looking for. The next version has to report two forms of the comparison and measure the ceiling effect instead of ignoring it.

decisions.plain: Some healthy reference cells exist only as cells grown in a dish, and growing in a dish changes their switch pattern. We measured which sites drift and we ignore them. That list is the mask. We kept the larger version on purpose: ignoring sites can only cost us sensitivity, never manufacture a result.

Brain cells: our healthy reference uses cleanly sorted cells only. How a sample was prepared moved the numbers more than the donor's age or the part of the brain did, so mixed preparations are out. This rule was changed after seeing that, which is why it is written down and sealed before either independent laboratory is opened.
When a sample's cell mixture cannot be verified, the chain withholds the reading instead of printing it. A number we cannot stand behind is worse than no number.

A data set we have already read cannot serve as the test of something new. Four of our planned test sets turned out to have been read before, so the rule is now enforced by code: a push is refused if a record names an already-read set as its held-out test.
